chapters.title: Chapter 6: Tax, the Buy Decision and Your Portfolio

lessons.title: How Property Is Taxed: Rental Income and Capital Gains

children.text: Anita bought a 2BHK in Baner, Pune for ₹60 lakh in 2016 and sells it in 2026 for ₹1.2 crore. Her profit looks like ₹60 lakh. Her tax bill could be about ₹6.3 lakh or about ₹7.4 lakh depending on one choice she makes, and close to zero if she reinvests correctly. Property tax in India rewards people who understand the rules and quietly penalises those who do not. This lesson covers the two ways property income is taxed: rent while you hold, and capital gains when you sell.

body.text: Property is taxed twice over its life: every year on the rent it earns, and once when you sell it for a gain. Planning for both before you buy can change your real return by lakhs.

body.label: A new Income-tax Act from 1 April 2026
body.value: Sections renumbered, core property rules largely unchanged
body.context: The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and introduced the term "tax year" in place of previous year and assessment year. House property provisions now sit mainly in Sections 20 to 25, and the familiar Section 54 and 54EC exemptions have new numbers. This lesson uses plain-English names so the ideas stay clear whatever the numbering.

markDefs.definition: Rent received or receivable in the year, minus municipal taxes actually paid by the owner. The starting point for taxing rental income.

children.text: Rent is taxed under "Income from House Property" at your slab rate. You start with the rent, subtract municipal property tax to reach the
, take a flat 30% standard deduction for repairs, and subtract interest on any loan taken for the property. You saw a full worked example of this in Chapter 3.

body.caption: The 30% standard deduction is allowed regardless of actual repair spending. Maintenance, brokerage and painting bills are not separately deductible.

body.title: Taxable rent
body.prompt: Rohit rents out a flat in Salt Lake, Kolkata for ₹25,000 a month for the full year and pays ₹10,000 in municipal property tax. The flat has no loan. What is his taxable income from house property, in ₹?
body.explanation: Rent: ₹25,000 × 12 = ₹3,00,000. Net annual value: ₹3,00,000 minus ₹10,000 = ₹2,90,000. Less 30% standard deduction of ₹87,000. Taxable income: ₹2,03,000, taxed at his slab rate.

body.text: Owning three or more homes can create tax on rent you never received. Beyond two self-occupied homes, the rest are treated as let out, and tax is charged on a reasonable expected rent even if the flat sits empty. Investors who buy several flats "for the future" are often surprised by this.

children.text: Indexation raises your purchase cost in line with inflation using the

body.text: Indexation saves Anita about ₹1.04 lakh here, because her flat grew at only a moderate pace. The rule of thumb: when a property's price has risen much faster than inflation, 12.5% without indexation tends to win; when growth was closer to inflation, 20% with indexation tends to win. Always calculate both.

body.title: Calculate an indexed cost
body.prompt: Suresh bought a flat in FY 2012-13 (CII 200) for ₹40 lakh and sells it in FY 2026-27 (CII 384). What is his indexed cost of acquisition, in ₹ lakh? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹40 lakh × 384 ÷ 200 = ₹76.8 lakh. If he sells for ₹1 crore, his indexed gain is ₹23.2 lakh, taxed at 20% (₹4.64 lakh), compared with a ₹60 lakh gain at 12.5% (₹7.5 lakh) without indexation.

children.text: Legal Ways to Save Tax on a Property Sale

body.caption: Main capital gains exemptions for long-term gains on property (simplified)

cells: Reinvest in a residential house (formerly Section 54)
Sell a residential house and buy another within 1 year before or 2 years after the sale, or construct one within 3 years
Exemption capped at ₹10 crore of investment; property must be held for 3 years
Two-house option
Invest the gain in two residential houses instead of one
Only if the gain is ₹2 crore or less, and only once in a lifetime
Specified bonds (formerly Section 54EC)
Invest the gain in notified bonds, such as those of NHAI, REC, PFC or IRFC, within 6 months of the sale
Maximum ₹50 lakh; 5-year lock-in
Selling other assets to buy a house (formerly Section 54F)
Sell a long-term asset like land or shares and invest the net sale proceeds in a residential house
Conditions on other houses owned; ₹10 crore cap
Capital Gains Account Scheme
Deposit unused gains in a designated bank account before the return filing due date, if you have not yet bought
Must be used within the allowed period, or the gain becomes taxable

body.title: Partial exemption through bonds
body.prompt: Anita chooses 12.5% without indexation, giving a long-term gain of ₹58.82 lakh. She invests the maximum ₹50 lakh in eligible bonds within 6 months and does not buy another house. On how much gain, in ₹ lakh, does she still pay tax?
body.explanation: ₹58.82 lakh minus ₹50 lakh = ₹8.82 lakh remains taxable. At 12.5%, that is about ₹1.10 lakh before surcharge and cess, down from ₹7.35 lakh. The cost is locking ₹50 lakh in bonds for 5 years at a modest interest rate, which is itself taxable.

body.title: Short or long term?
body.question: Kavitha bought a flat in Indore in March 2025 and sells it in January 2027 for a profit. How is her gain taxed?
options: Short-term, at her income tax slab rate
Tax-free, because it is a residential property
body.explanation: March 2025 to January 2027 is about 22 months, which is 24 months or less. The gain is short-term and added to her income at slab rates. Holding just a few more months would have made it long-term.

body.title: The holding period
body.textWithBlank: For land and buildings, a gain is long-term if the property was held for more than ___ months.
body.explanation: Property held for more than 24 months qualifies for long-term capital gains treatment. Listed shares and equity funds use a shorter 12-month threshold.

body.title: Anita's full plan
body.scenario: Anita, a resident, has sold her Baner flat with a long-term gain. She is considering three options: pay the tax and keep the cash, buy a smaller flat in Wakad for ₹70 lakh within a year, or put ₹50 lakh into eligible bonds.
body.prompt: How should she think about each option?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Choose the calculation first: as a resident who bought before 23 July 2024, she should compute both the 12.5% and 20% indexed options. The indexed option gives a lower tax of about ₹6.31 lakh versus ₹7.35 lakh.
2. Pay the tax and keep the cash: simplest, fully liquid, and lets her invest the rest freely.
3. Buy the Wakad flat: reinvesting in a residential house can exempt the gain up to the amount invested, and ₹70 lakh exceeds either calculation of the gain, so the gain could be fully exempt. But she must hold the new flat for 3 years, and she takes on fresh stamp duty of about 7% in Pune, plus all the concentration and illiquidity risks of property.
4. Invest in bonds: up to ₹50 lakh exempts that much of the gain, but it locks money for 5 years at a modest, taxable interest rate.
5. Combination: she can use the house and bond routes together, subject to the conditions.
6. Don't let tax drive the decision: saving ₹6 to 7 lakh of tax is not worth buying a property she does not otherwise want. She should decide on the investment first, then optimise tax, ideally with a tax professional's help.

body.title: Before Selling a Property
steps: Check whether you have held it for more than 24 months
Collect purchase deed, stamp duty and improvement cost receipts
If bought before 23 July 2024 and you are a resident, calculate both the 12.5% and 20% indexed options
Check the stamp duty value of the sale, since a sale below it beyond the tolerance changes the gain
Decide whether to use house reinvestment, bonds or the Capital Gains Account Scheme, and note the deadlines
Plan for TDS: resident buyers deduct 1% above ₹50 lakh; purchases from NRIs attract higher TDS
Consult a tax professional before signing the sale deed

cards.definition: Rent minus municipal taxes paid; the base for taxing rental income.
A flat deduction from net annual value for rental income, allowed regardless of actual repair costs.
A property beyond two self-occupied homes, taxed on notional rent even if vacant.
A gain on property held for more than 24 months, taxed at 12.5%, or 20% with indexation for eligible residents.
A yearly number used to adjust purchase cost for inflation; 376 for 2025-26 and 384 for 2026-27.
Investing up to ₹50 lakh of long-term gains in notified bonds within 6 months, with a 5-year lock-in.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 term for the financial year in which income is earned, replacing previous year and assessment year.

points: Rent is taxed at slab rates after deducting property tax and a flat 30% standard deduction, plus eligible loan interest.
Owning more than two self-occupied homes means tax on notional rent, even for empty flats.
Property held over 24 months gives long-term gains, taxed at 12.5% without indexation.
Residents selling property bought before 23 July 2024 can choose 20% with indexation, using CII values such as 384 for 2026-27.
Reinvesting in a residential house, specified bonds or the Capital Gains Account Scheme can reduce or eliminate the tax, subject to limits and deadlines.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 renumbered these provisions from April 2026 but kept their core logic; always calculate options before selling.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Tax rules, rates, section numbers and index values change and depend on your residential status, regime choice and specific facts. Figures exclude surcharge and cess. Consult a qualified tax professional before buying, renting out or selling property.
